the_claim_now_published.artifact: the published bytes are the artifact; the recipe is not. It fixes composition, widths and byte budget exactly and does not fix the weights.
the_claim_now_published.sibling: a rebuild is a sibling of the published checkpoint -- same composition, same widths, same byte budget, different trellis payloads. A different valid artifact of the same recipe, not a broken one.
the_claim_now_published.fidelity: every published fidelity number measures the bytes a downloader receives, so none of them is affected. What no longer holds is 'rebuild this and you get our numbers', which is now an untested expectation.
the_claim_now_published.floor: a byte diff against a published tree is not evidence of tampering, corruption or a changed recipe until it exceeds this floor; the checkable claim is the digest of the published tree (SHA256SUMS), not the output of a rebuild.
the_claim_now_published.environment: the recorded build environment provably could not have completed this conversion -- the pinned image has no marisa_trie and the recipe imports it twice on unconditional paths -- so the published environment record is incomplete and the conversion-capable image is gg-r34-convert. docs29_prose_for_main:
## Converter determinism — measured, and it changes what "reproduce" can mean

A fresh conversion of the published hydrated recipe, on the same box with the same flags and
the same source, does **not** return the published checkpoint. 13 of the 16 pinned payload
files come back identical — every config, the tokenizer, the safetensors index,
`quantization_config.json`, `quantization_manifest.json` — and the three safetensors shards do
not. The difference reaches tensor bytes and stops there: byte-identical headers, the same
2,426 physical tensors with the same names, dtypes, shapes and offsets, the same three-shard
packing to the byte. 399 tensors differ, every one a `.trellis` payload — 399 of the 409
quantized modules, 97.6 %, with 41-92 % of the bytes differing inside each, mean 82 %. No
scale, norm, embedding, vision or BF16 companion tensor moved, and everything a recipe fixes
came out exact: all ten per-role byte totals, 21,586,964,548 B of payload, 1,199 logical
tensors, 715 `tensor_storage` entries, every assigned width. The mechanism was measured, not
inferred: a failed first attempt left one log holding the same conversion twice, minutes apart,
with identical widths and identical global scales but different `proxy_err` for 6 of the 212
modules the comparison reaches. Two identical float computations round identically, so the
converter is nondeterministic. `receipts/converter-determinism.json`.

**Consequence 1 — the published bytes are the artifact, the recipe is not.** The recipe fixes
composition, widths and byte budget exactly and does not fix the weights, so a rebuild is a
sibling of the published checkpoint rather than the checkpoint: a different valid artifact of
the same recipe, not a broken one. Every published fidelity number measures the bytes a
downloader receives and is unaffected. What no longer holds is any "rebuild this and you get
our numbers" reading — that is now an expectation to test, and it is untested.

**Consequence 2 — there is a floor under byte comparisons.** A diff between a rebuild and a
published tree cannot be read as tampering, corruption or a changed recipe until it exceeds
this floor, and the checkable claim is the digest of the published tree — each repo's
`SHA256SUMS` — rather than the output of anyone's conversion. This lands directly on
**P0 / rank 3 — clean-room release reproduction**: rung 2 still stands as written, but its
acceptance clause "build differences are either byte-identical or explicitly reduced to a
measured numerical equivalence contract" now has a dead first branch. For a rebuilt checkpoint
the only reachable acceptance is the equivalence contract, and the contract needs a stated
tolerance: identical composition, widths, per-role byte totals, tensor names, dtypes, shapes,
offsets and shard sizes, with trellis payload differences permitted up to the measured floor.
Nothing else about that item changes.

None of this touches the runtime's weight-reconstruction path (`reconstruct_fp8_slice`, the
reconstructed-prefill kernels), which turns stored trellis bytes back into weights at load. The
two senses of "reconstruction" have to stay apart wherever both appear.

**Loose end A — a complete environment record for future builds.** Separate finding from the
same run: the published build's environment is not reconstructible. This recipe reaches
`import marisa_trie` twice on unconditional paths, and the pinned image
`release-evidence-hydrated.json` records has no `marisa_trie`, so that image provably cannot run
the conversion to completion. Something in the published run supplied it and nothing recorded
what. The published environment record is therefore incomplete; the conversion-capable image is
`gg-r34-convert`, which installs the same verified wheel the rebuild used. What is owed is a
build-time environment record that is sufficient on its own — image digest plus every
dependency supplied beside it, captured at build time rather than reconstructed afterwards — so
the next build is re-enterable and not merely re-attemptable.

**Loose end B — does a sibling rebuild land inside our interval?** Open experiment, never run.
The sibling built for this measurement was never scored: scoring it answers a different question
than the one that was asked, and it was released with the rest of the working tree. The test is
cheap now that the shard-0 BF16 reference is published — one candidate capture plus one replay,
about 6 minutes of GPU on shard 0 — but it costs a full ~40-minute conversion first to have a
sibling to score. Until someone runs it, the honest statement on the cards is the one now
published: a sibling should land within measurement resolution, and that has not been tested.
